t: Why so many numbers begin with 1: Benford’s law
d: Pick a number from a river, a price list or a newspaper and it starts with 1 about 30% of the time. A bowl of doubling numbers shows why.

t: Scrabble’s 100 tiles versus the five-letter words we actually use
d: Scrabble has twelve Es and four Ss. In our list of 809 five-letter answers, S is the first letter of one word in six.

t: How many words do you know? About 42,000, and it depends what you count
d: A large online experiment put a number on the average adult’s vocabulary. The interesting part is the three different numbers hiding inside it.

t: How heavy is a web page? A median phone page is 18 Ziggle pages
d: Every page here has a weight limit. Here is what it is, and what the rest of the web weighs.

t: The rules of a crossword grid: who decided 15 by 15?
d: A daily crossword is a small square of black and white with a surprising amount of law behind it, much of it written by one woman in the 1940s.

t: The 44 numbers below a million that set a Collatz record
d: Most starting numbers fall to 1 in a few dozen steps. Forty-four of the first million each took longer than every number before it, up to 524 steps.

t: 43 quintillion ways to be wrong: the Rubik’s Cube by numbers
d: A sculptor’s teaching tool, 500 million sales, and a proof that every scramble can be solved in 20 moves.

t: Ten study tricks, ranked: the highlighter came last
d: A 55-page review judged ten popular ways to study. Two came out on top, and neither is the one most students reach for.

t: Square, double-pennant and everything in between: a flag primer
d: Only two national flags are square, one isn’t a rectangle at all, and flag fans have a five-rule test for good design.

t: Twelve pieces, 2,339 ways: the pentomino puzzle
d: There are exactly twelve shapes you can make from five squares. Packing them into a rectangle has a precise answer, and a famous method for finding it.

t: Wordle has been solved: 3.42 guesses on average, starting with SALET
d: Two operations researchers worked out the perfect Wordle strategy. Being perfect still takes more than three guesses.

t: QWERTY: the keyboard layout nobody chose on purpose
d: A newspaper editor, five years of fiddling, a manufacturing deal, and the myth that it was designed to slow you down.

t: Type faster by slowing down
d: 136 million keystrokes say the fastest typists aren’t the ones racing. They’re the ones who don’t have to go back.

t: Feedback that teaches
d: A 2007 review found feedback works best when it answers three questions. Every Ziggle end-of-level popup tries to.

t: Why the answer you found tastes better than the one you’re given
d: People paid 63% more for a storage box they’d built themselves. Then researchers tried making them wreck it.

t: Where 15.87% comes from: the optimal error rate is one standard deviation of noise
d: The “85% rule” is not a rounding of folk wisdom. It is a number that falls out of an equation, and it is the area of a bell curve.

t: There are exactly 880 four-by-four magic squares
d: A French civil servant counted them by hand in the seventeenth century. We checked it in thirty seconds, and found 7,040.

t: Why the last stamp feels urgent
d: Coffee drinkers bought faster as they got closer to a free cup, and a card with two “free” stamps got finished sooner.

t: Mixed practice looked worse on day one and won by day thirty
d: In a three-month maths experiment, shuffling the problems helped a little the next day and much more a month later.

t: Show me first: the case for worked examples
d: For beginners, studying a solved example can beat solving problems cold. For experts, it can get in the way. Ziggle tries to do both.

t: One missed day does not break a habit
d: The best study of real habit formation found that skipping a single day made almost no difference. That is why Ziggle’s streaks forgive.

t: A wandering mind: what 250,000 phone check-ins revealed
d: People’s minds wandered almost half the time they were awake, and they were less happy when they did.

t: Kaprekar’s routine from two to seven digits: what happens to each length
d: Four digits give one constant. We ran the routine on every number from two to seven digits long, 10 million starts in all, and the endings are far stranger.

t: The five-minute break, by the numbers
d: A 2022 review of 22 studies found short breaks leave people feeling livelier and less tired. Performance is a more complicated story.

t: Scaffolding: why the cube trainer teaches seven steps first
d: Good teaching holds up the parts you can’t do yet, then takes the support away. The cube coach is built on that idea.

t: Small wins: what 12,000 work diaries said about good days
d: Managers ranked “progress” last on a list of motivators. The diaries ranked it first by a mile.

t: The 82, the 62 and the 39: reading the habit study properly
d: The habit paper behind the “66 days” headline starts with 96 people and ends with 39 clean curves. Here is what happened in between.

t: The 10,000-hour rule started with thirty violinists
d: The famous study behind the famous number compared three groups of ten young violinists. What it actually found is stranger and more useful.

t: Seventeen clues, 800 processor-years: the hunt for the smallest Sudoku
d: How few numbers can a Sudoku start with and still have only one solution? Proving the answer took one of the biggest puzzle searches ever run.

t: Why the unfinished crossword nags you
d: A waiter, a famous 1927 study, and a 2025 meta-analysis that politely took half of it apart.

t: The 1888 contest that made touch typing famous
d: A typist who never looked at the keys beat a rival who used eight fingers. Touch typing has been taught one key at a time ever since.

t: Letter Lock and the maths of a good guess
d: Your first guess is worth up to 7.9 bits of information. Most of us waste about half of it. A friendly introduction to Claude Shannon.

t: Every four-digit number ends up at 6174
d: Pick almost any four digits, do one simple trick again and again, and you always land on the same number within seven steps.

t: It’s on the tip of my tongue
d: You know the word. You know it starts with S. You know it has two syllables. Here’s what’s happening, and how Word Cloud uses it.

t: Why “the” is everywhere: Zipf’s law in a million words
d: In one famous million-word collection the most common word is nearly 7% of everything, and the second is almost exactly half as common.

t: A shoebox of flashcards that changed studying
d: Sebastian Leitner’s 1972 card-box method is the simple idea behind the Review tab in Ziggle’s trainers.

t: Hailstone numbers: a simple rule nobody can prove
d: Halve it if it is even, triple it and add one if it is odd. Everyone who has tried ends at 1. Nobody knows why.

t: The 2,500-year-old memory trick that still works
d: A collapsed banquet hall, 40 days of practice, and why memory champions say they were born with ordinary memories.

t: Sleep on it: the overnight puzzle solver
d: People who slept were about twice as likely to spot a hidden shortcut in a puzzle as people who stayed awake.

t: The magical number was probably four, not seven
d: George Miller said an integer had been persecuting him. A later review suggests he had the number a little high, and that he knew it.

t: Eight queens: four billion ways to try, 92 that work
d: A chess composer posed it in 1848. Counting the answers has been a favourite exercise ever since.

t: From 176 tiny pictures to 3,953 emoji
d: A pager heart, a phone company in Japan, a museum, and why your calendar emoji says July 17.

t: What the best violinists did besides practising: naps, 80-minute sessions and sleep
d: The 1993 study behind the 10,000-hour rule also logged a week of the violinists’ lives. The diaries say more about rest than about hours.

t: Stars, not scores: why trainers have a pass mark
d: In 1968 Benjamin Bloom argued that most learners can master a topic if they move on only once they’ve got it. Ziggle’s trainers work that way.

t: The 10,000-hour rule, and what it got wrong
d: It sold a lot of books. The researchers behind the original study weren’t fans. Here’s what practice actually explains.

t: One in twelve men and the colours of a puzzle
d: Colour-blind players are not a niche. We measured the contrast of our own palette to see where it stands.

t: 52 cards, 80 unvigintillion orders, and why sort() is not a shuffle
d: A well-shuffled deck is almost certainly in an order that has never existed before. A lazy shuffle in code can be wildly unfair, and we measured it.

t: Why the hard way feels worse and works better
d: The psychologist Robert Bjork has a name for practice that feels slow and sticks: desirable difficulties.

t: What chess masters see that you don’t (yet)
d: Masters remembered real chess positions far better than novices. Scramble the pieces at random and the gap shrank. That’s chunking.

t: Sudoku, arrows and the joy of the next obvious move
d: A retired architect, a Japanese name change, and 6.67 sextillion grids. Why logic puzzles feel so good to finish.

t: The birthday paradox, and why daily puzzles are never picked at random
d: In a room of 23 people, two probably share a birthday. The same sums explain why a “random” daily puzzle would repeat within weeks.

t: The safest data is the data we never collect
d: Ziggle needs no account, sets no cookies and has no trackers. Here’s what that means in practice, and what it costs us.

t: Monty Hall: the answer changes if the host doesn’t know
d: Switching wins two times in three, when the host knows where the car is. When he doesn’t, it makes no difference at all.

t: The sweet spot: getting it right about 85% of the time
d: A 2019 paper found a surprisingly precise number for how often learning should go wrong. We read the small print too.

t: A fifth of our five-letter answers end in E
d: We counted every letter of Letter Lock’s 809 answers. The numbers are lopsided in ways you can use.

t: Why so many of our buttons are 44 pixels tall
d: A 1954 experiment about moving a metal stylus explains why small buttons feel hard to hit, and why doubling a button saves exactly one bit.

t: Mix it up: why eight different puzzles beat eighty of one
d: Shuffled maths homework did “vastly” better a week later. Your puzzle habit can use the same trick.

t: Inside the experiment: 200 students, four ways to study, one surprise
d: A close reading of Karpicke and Blunt (2011): how the two experiments were built, what they measured, and the numbers that did not make the headlines.

t: What word games are really training
d: A 1913 newspaper filler, a game built for one person’s partner, and the mental move study researchers love most.

t: Leaderboards you can trust
d: A top score is only fun if it’s real. Ziggle’s server replays every run before it joins the board.

t: Quiz yourself: the study method that beat the fancy diagram
d: Students were sure concept maps would win. A week later, plain old recall had won by a mile.

t: The best gap between reviews: what 1,350 people taught us
d: Reviewing sooner or later changes how much you keep. One big experiment found the sweet spot, and that it shrinks the longer you want to remember.

t: Counting queens up to 14: the sequence, its ratios and a formula that is far off
d: We counted every n-queens solution up to a 14 × 14 board. The numbers climb about fivefold per step, and the formula for large boards says something else for small ones.

t: Five minutes a day: how small habits actually stick
d: The “21 days to a habit” rule is made up. Here’s what the studies found, and why your streak has freezes.

t: The best first guess in Letter Lock (we tried all 5,049)
d: A good first guess removes nearly everything. A bad one barely scratches the list. Here is the data from our own word lists.

t: The open dictionary inside Word Builder
d: It has 120,630 meanings, built by volunteers and given away free. Here is how a dictionary of meanings differs from a dictionary of spellings.

t: The Tower of Hanoi and the end of the world
d: A Victorian mathematician invented a legend to sell a puzzle. The sums behind it are real, and gloriously large.

t: The forgetting curve is real, and it’s beatable
d: In the 1880s a German psychologist memorised nonsense for five years so you wouldn’t have to. Here’s what he found.

t: The knight’s tour, and the count that was wrong for a year
d: A knight can visit every square of a chessboard once. How many ways? A famous published answer turned out to be more than double the truth.

t: Will puzzles make you smarter?
d: Short answer: no. The longer answer is better news, and it fits in a coffee break.

t: Streaks that forgive
d: Losing a streak hurts more than building one feels good. That’s why Ziggle’s streak has rest days, and why any one daily counts.

t: The typing teacher who never existed
d: Millions learned to type with Mavis Beacon. There was no Mavis Beacon. What the most famous typing tutor got right anyway.

t: The 1880 puzzle craze, and the arrows that followed
d: A sliding-tile toy once gripped America. Its descendants, from Rush Hour to Arrow escape, all ask one question: what has to move first?

t: Pelmanism, shell games and the sneaky shuffle
d: Memory Mischief borrows from two old tricks: turning over pairs of cards, and keeping your eye on the moving cup.

t: Why Ziggle has an ending
d: The inventor of infinite scroll has said he regrets it. Every Ziggle page, and every day, is built to finish.

t: Six numbers and a target
d: A French TV show from 1965 gave the world its favourite arithmetic race. Sum Spark keeps the puzzle and drops the clock.

t: Bulls, cows and the five-letter lock
d: Letter Lock belongs to a family of guessing games that is older than most of the board games in your cupboard.

t: No ads over the board
d: The rules Ziggle follows about advertising: where a promotion can sit, and what it never does.

t: Sudoku was born in Indiana
d: The “Japanese” number puzzle started life in an American magazine as Number Place, and needed two more countries to become famous.

t: Who invented the word search?
d: A small-town Oklahoma newsletter, a Spanish puzzle writer, and a game that looks simpler than it is.
